A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PC-Talk, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 includes supplementary Sections A–I; v3 ends with references while referring to an unavailable supplement for loss functions and implementation details. The main texts support reliable comparison, but supplementary completeness is unequal.

before.justification: v1 reports original HDTF/MEAD experiments, component ablations, qualitative demonstrations and a user study in supplementary Table S4.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, revised ablations, control sensitivity and interpolation experiments, efficiency measurements and the retained user study.

M1.justification: v1 uses preset one-hot speaking styles and leaves direct reference-video style extraction as future work in Appendix H. v3 Section 3.2 introduces video and preset encoders sharing a style space, mixed-source training and a discriminative style loss. It also reports revised LAC and EMC training objectives, substantially extending the method.

E1.justification: HDTF, MEAD and demonstrations on stylized faces remain. v3 Figure 1 adds a demonstrated reference-video speaking-style transfer scenario, which v1 treated as future work. v3 no longer documents CelebA-HQ/FFHQ augmentation, but this omission does not establish that those training sources were actually abandoned.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds LatentSync and Sonic and removes AniPortrait, updating the existing comparison groups. The qualitative comparison also replaces MuseTalk with LatentSync and omits AniPortrait/EchoMimic while adding Sonic. The emotional-generation and user-study comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The stated disjoint-split policy, 10-second cross-identity tests, 25-fps/16-kHz preprocessing and primary metrics remain. v3 adds parameter-sweep and efficiency evaluation procedures and reports two days of LAC training, versus v1's 24-hour predictor and 72-hour refiner stages. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish reruns or directly comparable training-cost improvements.

E4.justification: Table 3 changes from testing lip-related keypoints, the lip refiner and augmentation to testing the audio-visual encoder, synchronization loss and keypoint loss. v3 additionally introduces control-scale sensitivity, emotion/style interpolation and control-overhead analyses in Figures 5–6 and Table 4. The emotion-subtraction ablation is retained as Figure 4.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's newly stated user-study participant count and MOS protocol add study documentation without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds LatentSync/Sonic results, replacement ablation scores of 6.23/7.17/8.92/9.37 LSE-C, sensitivity curves and efficiency measurements. AniPortrait and the image-input no-augmentation row disappear from Table 1; MuseTalk's MEAD FID changes from 39.99 to 40.03. PC-Talk's retained primary scores and user-study scores remain unchanged apart from rounding. The replacement ablations use different configurations, so their scores do not establish a performance gain under unchanged conditions.

T1.justification: The reported mathematical loss specifications change: v1 Appendix D, Equation 14 uses an L2 keypoint norm, whereas v3 Section 3.4 describes Lkp as L1; v3 Equation 6 also introduces the style-loss term into the LAC objective. The keypoint construction and emotion-subtraction equations remain equivalent. Further loss-definition comparison is limited by the unavailable v3 supplement.

C1.justification: The central claims of precise speaking-style/emotion control and strong HDTF/MEAD performance remain. v3 broadens the speaking-style contribution to direct reference-video adaptation alongside presets and reframes word-level editing as articulation-specific control. This extends one contribution without replacing the overall research claim.

C2.justification: v3 interprets interpolation as evidence of a consistent style space and introduces practical control boundaries: editing remains stable around 0.8–1.2, with articulation-dependent sensitivity. It also discusses control overhead. v1's Appendix E/H qualifications about phoneme coupling and large-pose/cross-identity disentanglement are not available in the supplied v3 text.

D1.justification: v3 adds RTX 4090 hardware, 512×512 output resolution, EMC training duration, a project-page pointer and MOS details: 10 clips per method, durations over five seconds, over 20 participants and a 1–5 scale. Conversely, v1's explicit checkpoint initialization, 50/5-frame windows, augmentation filtering, Kalman filtering and named emotion encoders are not supplied in v3. Reproducibility documentation changes substantially, without proving those components were removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially updates positioning around recent generative approaches, computational efficiency and flexible control. New works include Sonic, LatentSync, Ditto, DiceTalk, MultiTalk and WAN; earlier discussions citing StyleSync, Follow-your-Emoji and other methods disappear. This revises the research context beyond citation renumbering or publication updates.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Training losses are consolidated in Section 3.4, evaluation metrics move into experimental settings, and dedicated Analysis and User Study sections are introduced. The user study moves from v1 Appendix G into the main text; terminology shifts toward articulation-specific control and compound emotions.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn to show reference-style input and the revised LAC structure, and the main qualitative comparison changes panels. v3 adds a sensitivity plot, interpolation figure and efficiency table, while resizing and relocating the user-study table. The emotion-subtraction figure is retained and renumbered; v1's augmentation diagram and supplementary result panels are absent from the supplied v3.

improvement.justification: v3 adds reference-style adaptation, newer baselines, useful sensitivity/efficiency evidence and clearer user-study documentation. However, the supplied PDF lacks substantial implementation, loss-definition and limitations material available in v1, while deferring essential new details to an unavailable supplement. Retained primary scores also leave the empirical effect of the revised method unresolved. These benefits and documentation gaps prevent a reliable judgment of the net change in paper quality.
